papers.title: Predicting the long-term impact of AI assistants on collective intelligence
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can improve individual performance but may weaken unaided performance and limit interest diversity, raising questions about their long-term effects on collective intelligence (CI). Here, we consider an evolutionary model in which individuals predict, consult AI, and imitate better-performing peers. Classic reward structures that promote CI without AI can fail under Chatbot AI, whose predictions depend on users' interests, by reducing interest diversity or propagating bias. Directly rewarding or penalizing AI use does not reliably mitigate these effects. Instead, a balanced incentive that preserves minority expertise and rewards collective contributions can promote CI, but an additional incentive is needed to restore unaided collective accuracy. Our framework offers an explanation for emerging evidence of AI's societal impact and clarifies its long-term implications.

papers.title: Notch1 and Notch2 receptors mediate the prosensory functions of the Notch ligand Jagged1 in the mammalian cochlea
papers.abstract: Mechanosensory hair cells in the cochlea of the inner ear are essential for sound detection. Previous studies have shown that loss of the Notch ligand Jagged1 (JAG1) disrupts maintenance of prosensory progenitors, from which hair cells and their surrounding supporting cells derive. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which JAG1 regulates prosensory progenitor maintenance are poorly understood, and the Notch receptors that mediate this function in the developing cochlea remain unknown. To address this, we generated Jag1 conditional knockout mice and characterized their prosensory deficits using transcriptomic and phenotypic analyses. We show that JAG1 loss abolishes prosensory expression of CDKN1B (p27Kip1) and reduces expression of essential neurotrophic factors, thereby disrupting the stereotyped pattern of cell-cycle exit and innervation within the prosensory domain. Furthermore, conditional knockout of Notch1 and Notch2 (Notch1/2) receptors in supporting cells phenocopied the Jag1 deletion phenotype, showing both a severe reduction in outer hair cell formation and a disrupted pattern of cell-cycle exit and innervation, thereby confirming their essential roles in mediating the prosensory functions of JAG1.

papers.title: A regenerative fibroblast competence field supports multiple cell fates in adult skin regeneration
papers.abstract: Adult mammalian wounds typically restore tissue integrity through fibrotic repair rather than regeneration of the original architecture. Here, we compared small non-regenerative and large regenerative skin wounds to investigate how fibroblasts acquire regenerative competence and enter alternative cell-fate programs. Integrated single-cell RNA sequencing identified a transient signaling and extracellular-matrix-remodeling niche enriched in large wounds, together with NCAM1-associated competent fibroblast states. Time-resolved analysis positioned these states within a root-like fibroblast manifold connected to hair dermal-condensate, endothelial, pericyte and glial-associated fate-entry programs. Inferred cell-cell communication networks revealed shared matrix and adhesion signals, superimposed with branch-associated inputs, including VEGF signaling toward NCAM1-positive endothelial-transition cells. Lineage tracing showed that PDGFRA- and NCAM1-expressing lineages contributed to vascular- and nerve/glial-associated regenerative compartments. Functionally, partial NCAM1 perturbation reduced vascular organization while increasing hair follicle neogenesis, whereas stronger inhibition impaired both outcomes. These findings identify NCAM1 as a regulator of regenerative competence and fate specification within a regenerative competence field rather than a marker of a single terminal lineage. We propose that regenerative wounds activate an NCAM1-associated fibroblast competence field whose quantitative modulation biases competent fibroblasts toward alternative outcomes.

papers.title: A possible role for the kinetochore COMA complex in sensing the damage in stn1-sz2, a mutant of the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 telomeric complex
papers.abstract: Telomeres, the ends of linear chromosomes, form a cap composed of specific telomeric DNA associated with specialized proteins that ensures efficient protection against chromosome degradation and, consequently, overall genome instability. Three main complexes have been implicated in chromosome end protection, namely telomerase, shelterin, and the CST complex (CTC1/Cdc13-STN1-TEN1). In a recent study, we uncovered mutants of the S. cerevisiae CST in which damage was sensed both by the two major spindle checkpoints and the major DNA damage checkpoint. In the best-studied of these mutants, stn1-sz2, the stability and organization of the mitotic tubulin spindle was profoundly affected, as were the organization of the centrosomes and the kinetochores. Here, we find that the stn1-sz2 mutant is hypersensitive to deletion mutants of two members of the kinetochores, Ctf19 and Mcm21, which correlated with mis-localization of their associated subunit in the COMA complex, Okp1, during anaphase. Defects in interactions between the kinetochores and the tubulin spindle are entirely sensed by the SAC (spindle assembly checkpoint). Here, we find that some of the stn1-sz2 damage is recognized by the Mad2 checkpoint protein independently from the SAC. The data presented here contribute to a better understanding of the damage in stn1-sz2, the prototype of novel mutants of telomeric CST characterized by mitotic-spindle-damage in addition to the classical telomeric-DNA-damage.

papers.title: Endothelial gain of PIEZO/TRPV mechanosensors drives cavernous malformations
papers.abstract: Vascular disease often begins as a failure to read mechanical force. Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are leaky, brain-invading capillary clusters that cause stroke and seizures and arise from endothelial loss of the CCM complex. They form exclusively in low-flow vessels but existing models cannot explain this selectivity. We previously established that CCM-mutant endothelium inverts its adhesive balance, weakening cell-cell junctions while building matrix-degrading adhesions. The mechanosensors imposing this switch are unknown. Here we show that the mechanosensitive Ca2+ channels PIEZO1, TRPV2 and TRPV4 are overexpressed in the endothelium of CCM lesions in a 42-patient cohort, and that lesion volume scales with their expression level. Mechanistically, PIEZO1 partners with TRPV4 to destabilise cell-cell junctions and with TRPV2 to reinforce cell-matrix adhesions; silencing TRPV4 restores junctional integrity and abolishes KLF4 induction, whereas silencing TRPV2 or inhibition with tranilast abolishes matrix degradation and invasion. In vivo, trpv4 knockdown or inhibition with GSK2798745 restores atrioventricular canal morphogenesis in ccm2-mutant zebrafish. Gain of mechanosensory channel function is thus a causal step in CCM pathogenesis, upstream of the KLF program. Combined therapeutic targeting of TRPV2 and TRPV4 with inhibitors validated in humans offers a route to therapy.

papers.title: Transient 5-azacytidine exposure elicits persistent myogenic-like transcriptional remodeling in zebrafish fibroblasts: implications for cultivated seafood
papers.abstract: Fibroblasts are readily obtained and expanded and may provide an alternative cell source for cultivated seafood if their latent myogenic potential can be accessed. We examined whether transient exposure to 5-azacytidine (AZA), a cytidine analogue known to convert mouse embryonic fibroblasts into myoblasts, elicits a persistent muscle gene program in embryo-derived zebrafish (Danio rerio) Z3 fibroblasts. Cells were exposed to 0, 2.5, 5 or 10 M AZA for 48 h and maintained in drug-free medium for 3 weeks. RNA-seq identified 744 genes that increased and 670 that decreased consistently across the concentration series. Increased genes encompassed myogenic regulators, fusion factors, sarcomeric components and excitation-contraction machinery, whereas decreased genes were enriched for extracellular-matrix and adhesion functions. In a separate six-dose RT-qPCR experiment (0-20 M AZA) with three biological replicates per concentration, all 19 selected muscle genes were significantly increased at 1.25 M, the lowest concentration tested, whereas 9 of 12 extracellular-matrix/fibroblast genes were significantly decreased. Several muscle genes plateaued or declined at higher concentrations, and multinucleated myotubes were not observed. A separate 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine (decitabine) series showed a comparable muscle-associated response at 0.25 M. These findings indicate that zebrafish fibroblasts retain access to a myogenic-like transcriptional program, and they provide a model for identifying food-compatible approaches to control fish-cell lineage plasticity for cultivated seafood.

papers.title: AI-assisted quantification of the clonogenic assay
papers.abstract: The clonogenic assay is the foundational standard for evaluating cellular radiosensitivity, yet its manual quantification is limited by labor-intensive processing, high inter-observer variability, and a reductive binary scoring system. Here, we present and validate a deep learning-based segmentation pipeline for the automated, high-throughput quantification of mammalian cell survival across diverse radiation qualities (photons, protons, and carbon ions). By benchmarking against expert consensus using Bland-Altman analysis, we demonstrate that this AI framework consistently operates within natural human error margins. Crucially, transitioning to automated whole-well image-based analysis enables the extraction of continuous multidimensional data, including colony area, density, and cellularity. This phenotypic profiling successfully identified and quantified high-cellularity colonies formed by radioresistant BxPC-3 cells under particle irradiation. Coupled with rapid image acquisition platforms, this methodology significantly reduces processing bottlenecks while standardizing the derivation of relative biological effectiveness (RBE). By advancing beyond binary survival metrics to continuous morphological profiling, this framework provides a vital new analytical dimension for investigating structural mechanisms of radioresistance.

papers.title: An amyloid-β/APP regulatory layer in human brown adipocyte recruitment identifies repurposable drugs for thermogenic fat expansion
papers.abstract: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) increases energy expenditure but is scarce in adults, yet most strategies focus on activating existing thermogenic adipocytes rather than recruiting new ones. We integrate human single-nucleus transcriptomics with protein-interaction and knowledge-graph analyses to identify stage-specific, druggable programmes governing brown adipogenesis. This pipeline resolved four ordered transcriptional states and three transitions, revealing an amyloid-{beta}/APP regulatory layer and nominating APP as a central signalling hub. Most prioritised compounds altered differentiation or metabolic phenotype, several substantially. Phenserine (APP-lowering) and sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) promoted differentiation through distinct mechanisms and stages and could be combined sequentially for benefit. Phenserine increased differentiation across three human models and, in mice, expanded BAT mass and increased thermogenic capacity. Together, these findings reveal targetable control points in human brown adipocyte recruitment, nominate repurposable drugs for BAT expansion, and establish a generalisable framework coupling single-cell transcriptomics with network-based drug repurposing across staged biological systems.

papers.title: SETD3 ACTIN HISTIDINE METHYLTRANSFERASE REGULATES INTESTINAL EPITHELIAL BARRIER INTEGRITY AND MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION
papers.abstract: Intestinal epithelial barrier is a key feature of the healthy gut, and disruption of this barrier is a driver of mucosal inflammation. Integrity of the intestinal epithelial barrier is controlled by tight junctions (TJs) and adherens junctions (AJs) associated with the underlying actin cytoskeleton. Posttranslational modifications of actins affect the cytoskeletal assembly and dynamics, however whether such modifications regulate epithelial barriers remains unknown. SETD3 methyltransferase methylates actins at the His73 residue, thereby enhancing filamentous (F)-actin polymerization and turnover. This study examines the role of SETD3 in regulating structure and function of normal intestinal epithelial barrier, as well as its involvement in barrier disruption during mucosal inflammation. siRNA mediated knockdown of SETD3 in DLD-1 and HCA-7 human intestinal epithelial cells (IEC) resulted in several functional and morphological cell abnormalities. These include increased permeability of the IEC barrier, diminished assembly of the perijunctional F-actin belt, increased cell size, and delayed TJ reassembly during calcium switch. Consistently, SETD3 knockout (KO) mice displayed increased intestinal permeability and decreased labeling intensity of apical {beta}-actin as compared to wildtype controls. Furthermore, SETD3 KO mice showed increased cell stemness and proliferation in colonic epithelium without defects in AJ/TJ assembly and secretory cell differentiation. In addition, SETD3 KO mice developed more severe disease symptoms during dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis, which were accompanied by accelerated mucosal erosion and increased macrophage, T cell and neutrophil infiltration into colonic tissue. Overall, our data suggests that SETD3 acts as a novel positive regulator of the intestinal epithelial barrier and plays a protective role during intestinal mucosal damage and inflammation.

papers.title: Cajal bodies shape the nuclear transcriptome, intron retention and transcripts redistribution in Arabidopsis roots under hypoxia
papers.abstract: Cajal bodies (CBs) are nuclear condensates known for their role in sn- and snoRNA maturation in animal, but their function in plant stress responses remains poorly understood. We compared wild-type (WT) Arabidopsis thaliana with the CB-lacking ncb-1 mutant during hypoxia and reoxygenation, focusing on nuclear retention of transcripts. In both genotypes, hypoxia caused nuclear accumulation of poly(A+) RNA and extensive reprogramming of gene expression. However, the transcriptional response, including induction of hypoxia-responsive genes, was considerably weaker in ncb-1, both during stress and recovery. In nuclear RNA, introns with low (intron retention index, IRX 50%) retention showed opposite, genotype-dependent dynamics. During hypoxia, efficiently spliced introns (IRX < 10%) accounted for over 70% of introns detected in nuclear RNA. Relative to normoxia, this proportion increased two- to threefold in WT but only moderately in the mutant. Together with poly(A+) RNA accumulation, this suggests that largely spliced transcripts, including those of genes involved in protein transport and ribosome biogenesis, are held in the nucleus during stress. Conversely, strongly retained introns, often terminal and located in genes related to hypoxia and other abiotic stresses, were most abundant in WT nuclear RNA under normoxia. Their proportion dropped sharply during hypoxia, and much less so in ncb-1. This indicate that WT plants maintain a nuclear reserve of incompletely spliced stress-related transcripts that are processed upon stress. The mutant also showed reduced interaction between U2 snRNA and U2B'', which leads to splicing defects. Our results indicate that CBs regulate which transcripts are held in the nucleus and how they are processed, contributing to plant tolerance of oxygen deprivation and recovery.

papers.title: DLGAP5 promotes vascular cell proliferation and remodeling in pulmonary arterial hypertension
papers.abstract: Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) manifests by pulmonary vascular remodeling, caused by hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of resident PA cells, elevated right ventricular (RV) afterload, and death of RV failure. The goal of this study is to determine the role and mechanisms of action of mitotic spindle-associated microtubule regulator DLG associated protein 5 (DLGAP5) in pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH. Methods: DLGAP5 expression was assessed in human PAH transcriptomic datasets, PAH patients' lung tissues, pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs), and pulmonary artery adventitial fibroblasts (PAAFs). Loss-of-function, molecular, functional, RNAseq, and network analyses were performed. Smooth muscle (SM)-specific DLGAP5 knockdown using adeno-associated virus serotype 6 (AAV6) in mice with SU5416/hypoxia-induced PH was performed. Results: DLGAP5 was overaccumulated in small muscular PAs, PASMCs, and PAAFs from PAH lungs. siRNA DLGAP5 down-regulated cyclin A2, suppressed hyper-proliferation, increased pro-apoptotic BIM, and induced apoptosis in human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs. DEP domain containing 1 (DEPDC1) was identified and validated as a downstream effector of DLGAP5 in PAH PASMCs responsible for hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of human PAH PASMCs. SM-specific DLGAP5 knockdown with AAV6-enTagln-shDLGAP5 reversed DEPDC1 overaccumulation in small muscular PAs, reduced PA medial thickness, RV systolic pressure, mean PA pressure, and RV hypertrophy in mice with SuHx-induced PH. Conclusions: DLGAP5 supports proliferation and survival of human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs through up-regulation of cyclin A2, DEPDC1, and suppression of BIM, and promotes PA remodeling and PH in mice. DLGAP5 could serve as a potential molecular target to attenuate pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH.

papers.title: Fast single molecule localization microscopy in 3D
papers.abstract: Super-resolution methods, such as single molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM), can determine the distribution of specific proteins at the nanometre scale. However, three-dimensional (3D) SMLM is typically limited to thin sections and requires prohibitively long acquisition times to image complete cells. Here we introduce a 3D SMLM imaging modality, Intrinsic3D, that combines the speed and optical sectioning of oblique plane microscopy (OPM) with the nanometre resolution of SMLM to determine the position of single molecule emitters throughout complete volumes more than an order-of-magnitude faster over regular DNA-PAINT. By scanning the oblique light sheet across the volume and combining localization information from two or more adjacent planes, an emitter's x, y and z position is determined, eliminating the need for post-processing steps to stitch multiple image stacks together. We demonstrate resolution and speed by imaging nuclear pore complexes in U2OS cells and Drosophila egg chambers. As a proof-of-concept, we map the 3D distribution of the cell-adhesion protein DE-cadherin in the Drosophila follicular epithelium and show that spot adherens junctions are enriched near tricellular junctions and contain more E-cadherin than the apical adherens junctions, suggesting that spot junctions play a wider role in cell-cell adhesion than previously appreciated. Finally, we examine the organization of Gliotactin, a tricellular septate junction protein relative to E-cadherin using exchange-PAINT. These investigations demonstrate that Intrinsic3D delivers rapid 3D protein mapping in whole cells. Combining Intrinsic3D with existing multiplex and resolution enhancing methods (e.g. exchange-PAINT and RESI) will enable multicolour, 3D in situ spatial proteomics in tissue samples and bridge the gap between SMLM and systems-level cell biology.

papers.title: A two-step organoid screen identifies transient p53 activation as a senolytic strategy for radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction
papers.abstract: Radiotherapy significantly improves the survival of head and neck cancer patients. However, it frequently damages the salivary glands, causing persistent hyposalivation and xerostomia. Radiation-induced cellular senescence within the salivary gland stem/progenitor cell niche contributes to hyposalivation, suggesting that selective elimination of senescent cells could promote tissue recovery. However, the effectiveness of senolytic compounds is strongly context dependent, varying with tissue of origin and potentially impairing regenerative cells required for functional restoration. Here, we developed a two-step organoid-based screening methodology that integrates the preferential induction of apoptosis in irradiated, senescence enriched, salivary gland organoids with the preservation of stem/progenitor cell regenerative capacity. As a first step, the senolytic activity of candidate drugs was tested to identify drugs that induced apoptosis in senescent cells of irradiated organoids but were not or less toxic to unirradiated organoids. As a second step, the confirmed senolytic compounds were tested for effects on stem cell self-renewal potential. Using this approach, we identified Nutlin3a, an MDM2 inhibitor and p53 activator, as the compound with the most favorable toxicity profile in salivary glands. Last, we confirmed the anti-senescence and pro-regenerative potential of Nutlin3a in an in vivo mouse model of radiation-induced hyposalivation, where localized Nutlin3a delivery resulted in a robust increase in saliva production, as early as two weeks after administration. These findings establish an organoid-based strategy for identifying tissue-adapted senolytic interventions and propose transient local p53 activation with Nutlin3a as a potential approach to mitigate radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction.

papers.title: Dynamic membrane organization coordinates protein-O-mannosylation and proteostasis in mycobacteria.
papers.abstract: Integral membrane enzymes operate within molecular environments, yet how these are organized remains poorly understood. Using M. smegmatis as a mycobacterial model, we define the membrane environment of the protein O-mannosyltransferase MtPMT through stratified interactomics combining affinity purification-mass spectrometry under four stringencies with a persistence score. This approach resolves a persistent membrane-associated core of 108 proteins from more transient layers, revealing a hierarchically organized landscape enriched in Sec protein translocation, protein biogenesis and envelope proteostasis machineries. Reciprocal affinity purification and in vivo FRET identify YajC and FtsH as neighbors of MtPMT, while structural modelling supports integration within a Sec-associated assembly. Genetic disruption of factors reduces O-mannosylation activity, demonstrating dependence on platform integrity. The MtPMT-associated network is remodelled during growth, indicating an adaptive system. Loss of POM compromises envelope permeability and stress resilience, linking O-mannosylation to fitness. Together, our results establish protein O-mannosylation as an integrated component of a dynamic membrane platform coordinating secretion, membrane protein biogenesis and proteostasis. Our findings support a model in which mycobacterial membranes contain specialized domains dynamically modulated by physiological state.

papers.title: A Structural Model of Transcriptional Activation by Mediator
papers.abstract: Mediator integrates regulatory signals from transcription factors (TFs) and controls RNA polymerase II (Pol II) activity in eukaryotes. Its Tail module serves as the primary hub for TF activation domains (ADs), but the mechanistic logic coupling this distal engagement to transcriptional output is unclear. Here we model an extensive set of human AD-Tail interactions with AlphaFold 3 and infer how they may influence the architecture of the Mediator-Pol II complex. Across the ensemble, ADs recurrently engage a restricted set of surfaces spanning multiple Tail subunits, revealing several previously unrecognized sites. The ensemble map recovers established activator-binding regions and is consistent with prior biochemical and structural data. Our modeling suggests how multivalent AD binding modulates the conformational landscape of the Tail to favor an initiation-competent Pol II state, providing a structural framework for tunable gene activation through Mediator.

papers.title: A contact-mediated transfer mechanism directs in cis localization and spread of Xist RNA
papers.abstract: X chromosome inactivation in mammals is driven by the long non-coding RNA Xist, which localizes and spreads across the chromosome from which it is transcribed. Although several factors required for Xist localization have been identified, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine Nuclear-BRITE, a method for visualizing and quantifying the dynamics of individual Xist RNA molecules, with acute depletion of key localization factors. We find that Xist molecules remain constrained throughout interphase, consistent with continuous association with chromatin. Building on this observation, we identify a contact-mediated transfer mechanism in which 3D chromosome dynamics promote handover of Xist molecules between chromosomal sites. We further show that the Xist-binding proteins SPEN and HNRNPU play distinct roles in this process by promoting Xist - Xist and Xist - chromatin interactions, respectively. Together, our findings define a mechanism for Xist RNA spreading and provide a framework for understanding its unique chromosome-wide localization.

papers.title: The RNA helicase KREH2 directly binds the RESC1-RESC2 complex in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing
papers.abstract: Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo. We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5'-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.

papers.title: Ciliary neurotrophic factor curbs palmitate-induced inflammatory and metabolic changes in NPY/AgRP hypothalamic neurons
papers.abstract: Introduction: In both humans and experimental animals, obesity is associated with hypothalamic inflammation and neuronal metabolic dysfunction, which contribute to disrupting body energy homeostasis. Although ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) is a neuroprotective cytokine with recognized anti-obesity effects in peripheral metabolic tissues, its role in obesity-associated hypothalamic dysfunction is still poorly characterized. We investigated whether CNTF exerts any direct effects on mHypoE-N41 (N41) hypothalamic neurons and whether it modulates the effects induced by palmitate (PA), an established model of obesity-associated neuronal metabolic dysfunction. Methods: N41 cells were administered CNTF alone or combined with PA to assess whether CNTF affects PA-induced lipotoxic stress. Gene and protein expression was assessed by qRT-PCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence analysis. Results: In N41 cells, CNTF activated the STAT3, ERK and AMPK signaling pathways. It also upregulated genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and fatty acid oxidation, including Ucp2, Cpt1 and Pgc1, as well as the proliferation-associated markers Ki-67 and PCNA. PA treatment induced inflammatory and endoplasmic reticulum stress responses and impaired insulin signaling. In PA-treated N41 cells, CNTF significantly attenuated the expression of pro-inflammatory markers Tnf, Mcp1 and Nfkb, restored insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, and partially reversed PA-induced changes in the expression of metabolic genes Ucp2 and Cpt1. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings indicate that CNTF exerts direct protective metabolic effects on hypothalamic N41 neurons subjected to lipotoxic stress and supports a role for it in the preservation of neuronal metabolic function under obesogenic conditions.

papers.title: Extreme climatic events shape adaptive potential by altering genetic variance for adult survival in a wild population
papers.abstract: Extreme climatic events (ECEs) could potentially induce episodes of rapid adaptive evolution, altering the evolutionary trajectories and viability of wild populations experiencing increasingly stochastic environments. Adaptive potential stems substantially from additive genetic variance (V) in survival. However, the degree to which ECEs impact this variance, and the resulting evolutionary implications, have not been fully conceptualised or quantified in nature. These aims are highly challenging because underlying genetic and environmental variances have fundamentally non-linear effects on the dichotomous phenotypic outcome of survival versus death, while substantial data are required for estimation. We present a conceptual and analytical framework that formalises biological hypotheses for how V depends on environmental severity, how such dependences are reshaped by non-linear genotype-environment-phenotype relationships and demographic structure, and the implications for evolutionary responses. We then use 25 years of survival and pedigree data from European shags (Gulosus aristotelis) to decompose variance in adult survival across diverse environmental conditions including ECEs. Using a capture-recapture animal model, we demonstrate non-negligible V underlying adult survival across all years combined, implying notable adaptive potential. Yet, partitioning by environmental severity revealed substantial V in good years with high survival but negligible V in bad years with ECE-induced low survival, implying a genotype-by-environment interaction that constrains adaptive potential under severe conditions. However, scale transformations showed how the non-linear genotype-environment-phenotype relationship can distort or even reverse such patterns, by reducing the extent to which V is phenotypically expressed in good conditions with high mean survival and amplifying it in more severe conditions with lower mean survival. Evolutionary responses to severe conditions could consequently be non-negligible even given small underlying V. We thereby demonstrate how ECEs can reshape adaptive potential, highlighting the need to integrate impacts of environmental severity on genetic variation in fitness components into predictions of population resilience under climate change.

papers.title: Statistical inference of virus evolution using ancestral recombination graphs
papers.abstract: Ancestral recombination graphs (ARGs) represent the coalescent history at every locus in the genome, subject to mutation and recombination. Modelling viruses using the coalescent with recombination remains less explored, due to the potential for complex, multi-scale dynamics. Using perturbative methods, we establish mathematical bounds that describe the balance between inter-host and within-host coalescence, and demonstrate that the highly-recombinant Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) coalesces predominantly at the inter-host level. We then modify SINGER, a tool from diploid genetics, for haploid ARG inference with fine-grained variable recombination rates. We provide insight into the paradox of high recombination rates and slow linkage disequilibrium decay, as ARG-based methods potentially allow us to disentangle epistatic effects from shared ancestry, and illustrate this using the coalescent topologies of EBV's host cell-entry glycoproteins. Our findings demonstrate that ARG-based methods recover gene-level selective structure, and provide a general method for analysing virus phylodynamics in the limit of small quantities.

papers.title: Community-wide adaptive evolution of gut bacteria during dietary transitions
papers.abstract: Diet exerts selection on bacterial species within the mammalian gut microbiota1,2,3,4,5, but the extent, modes, genomic bases, and repeatability of gut bacterial adaptive evolution in response to dietary variation within hosts are poorly understood. Here, we show that within-host dietary transitions drive ubiquitous and highly reproducible adaptive evolution of gut bacterial populations. We deeply profiled allele-frequency dynamics in gut microbiota of an experimental cohort of litter-matched wild-derived isogenic mice either transitioned from low-fat/high-carbohydrate diets to high-fat/low-carbohydrate diets or maintained on their ancestral low-fat/high-carbohydrate diet. Dietary transitions induced significantly parallel allele-frequency changes across replicates in 61/62 core gut bacterial species within five months, whereas 0/62 species displayed significant across-replicate parallelism in the control group, indicating deterministic adaptive evolutionary responses across the gut microbiota. Adaptation proceeded through multiple modes, including strain sorting and gene-wise responses. The latter were enriched in a subset of gene families and functions across bacterial species, including invertases. Culturing revealed an invertible DNA switch in Phocaeicola sartorii that, in all replicates transitioned to high-fat/low-carbohydrate diets, localized a promoter sequence upstream of cell-surface glycan foraging genes. These findings elucidate widespread gut bacterial adaptive evolution mediated by within-host dietary variation.

papers.title: Genomic and phenotypic consequences of long-term isolation and small population size in Yakushima macaques
papers.abstract: The relative roles of genetic drift, inbreeding, and natural selection in island evolution have been fundamental themes in evolutionary biology for nearly a century. However, empirical studies have yet to reach a consensus, and research integrating both genotypes and phenotypes in primates remains limited. The present study aims to estimate the demographic history of an island primate population, the Yakushima macaque (Macaca fuscata yakui), and evaluate the genomic and morphological consequences of its isolation. To this end, we conducted population genetic analyses based on whole-genome sequencing and geometric morphometric analyses of cranial shape. Our results indicate that M. f. yakui has been isolated with an effective population size of several thousand individuals for over 100,000 years. Although we detected signatures of purifying selection, deleterious alleles have not been sufficiently purged. The degree of fluctuating asymmetry in males was slightly, yet significantly, higher in M. f. yakui than in mainland populations, whereas this trend was not observed in females. Marginal evidence of directional selection was found for cranial size, but not for shape. Overall, our findings suggest that due to long-term isolation, genetic drift and inbreeding have exerted a substantial influence on shaping genotypic and phenotypic variation in this island population.

papers.title: BRN2 suppresses stress-induced hair greying
papers.abstract: Adult stem cells maintain tissue homeostasis and regenerative capacity, but mechanisms preserving their integrity under stress remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify BRN2 (POU3F2), a POU-domain transcription factor, as a regulator of melanocyte lineage homeostasis and response to genotoxic stress. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified Brn2 among transcription factors preferentially active in melanocyte stem cells (McSCs), with BRN2 activity declining with age in human hair follicle melanocytic cells. Melanocyte-specific Brn2 deletion increased melanocyte differentiation and accumulation in the hair bulb, while downregulating DNA-repair and chromosome-maintenance programs. Despite these changes, Brn2 loss caused neither spontaneous hair greying nor detectable McSC depletion under steady-state conditions. Following ionizing radiation, however, Brn2-deficient cells showed altered DNA-damage responses, reduced mitotic signatures, increased p53 and p21, and enhanced melanocytic differentiation. Irradiated Brn2-deficient mice developed rapid, dose-dependent, permanent hair depigmentation associated with McSC and melanocyte depletion. Thus, BRN2 links POU-dependent transcriptional control to stem-cell resilience under genotoxic stress, preserving melanocyte regenerative capacity and protecting against irradiation-induced hair greying.

papers.title: Promoter-targeted duplex RNAs activate TCF4 expression
papers.abstract: Pitt-Hopkins syndrome (PTHS) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficient expression of transcription factor 4 (TCF4). Increasing expression from the remaining functional TCF4 allele could provide a mutation-independent strategy for patients with diverse pathogenic variants. We integrated genomic datasets with strand-specific RNA analysis to identify transcribed regions of the TCF4 promoter suitable for targeting by activating double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs). Screening of overlapping promoter-targeted dsRNAs identified a hotspot for increased TCF4 expression. Activation was retained by a lead dsRNA containing extensive 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methyl, and phosphorothioate modifications used in therapeutic oligonucleotides. Anti-AGO2 immunoprecipitation showed association with RNA transcribed from the targeted promoter region. dsRNA-mediated activation was associated with increased RNA polymerase II occupancy. These findings establish promoter-targeted dsRNAs as chemically tractable starting points for increasing TCF4 expression and support their investigation as a mutation-independent strategy for haploinsufficient disease.

papers.title: Epigenetic regulators partition the genome by evolutionary and developmental constraint
papers.abstract: Many epigenetic regulators play essential roles in animal development, but precisely how they function across different cell types without clear sequence preferences remains a foundational challenge. Here, we employed single-cell RNA sequencing to survey the mutant phenotypes of 30 essential regulatory pathways across over 450 gastrulation stage mouse embryo replicates, including essential factors associated with repressive chromatin states, RNA surveillance/processing, and other genomic roles. We then use this integrated manifold to partition mutant responses into a developmentally-resolved interaction network, revealing a hierarchy of heterochromatin-associated interactions that act orthogonally to Polycomb Repressive Complex-mediated control of embryo patterning. Compared to the embryo proper, we find that the developing placenta and yolk sac can accommodate broad swings in repetitive element expression, a resilience in keeping with the relative evolutionary recency and phenotypic plasticity of these tissues. Dense temporal sampling of Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) mutant embryogenesis further supports the notion that the gastrulating embryo is particularly constrained and depends on multiple layers of insulation, including the need to suppress evolutionarily young genetic elements to stably license highly conserved, phylotypic programs. In combination, our work highlights the power of single cell-resolved developmental genetics to contextualize the roles of epigenetic regulators, which restrict genomic action to support robust cellular identities and embryological forms.

papers.title: Optogenetic BMP4 models symmetry breaking and primitive streak formation in hPSCs
papers.abstract: Gastrulation begins when the epiblast epithelium breaks symmetry to form the primitive streak, but current in vitro models neither fully capture this process nor separate its mechanical and chemical inputs. Here, we introduce LightBMP, an optogenetic platform that enables spatiotemporally programmable BMP4 expression in human pluripotent stem cells. Dose and duration control reveal a sustained low-BMP regime, inaccessible to recombinant ligand, that specifies mesoderm. Spatially programmed BMP4 sources in uniform cultures mimic the radial organization of 2D gastruloids, showing that mechan-ical context and edge sensing are not required for patterning. In micropatterned colo-nies, light-defined sources break symmetry to generate a stripe-shaped, primitive-streak-like domain where cells acquire multiple mesodermal fates and undergo directed migration. Together, these results show that spatial control of a single morphogen source is sufficient to drive symmetry breaking and primitive-streak-like patterning, independent of edge constraints.

papers.title: microRNAs control temporal patterning of the vertebrate nervous system
papers.abstract: Temporal patterning is essential for generation of neuronal diversity in the developing vertebrate nervous system. A shared sequence of temporal transcription factors (tTFs) partitions neurons by birth date across much of the central nervous system. The molecular mechanisms that control the timing of expression of these tTFs are incompletely understood. Here, we provide evidence that this process is under the control of microRNAs (miRNAs). Perturbing miRNA biogenesis by conditional deletion of Dgcr8 from the developing mouse nervous system extends the window during which neurons with early identities are generated, but abolishes late identities in the spinal cord, hindbrain and midbrain, and holds progenitors in an early transcriptional state. We further identify miRNAs of the let-7 and miR-9 families, which target transcriptional regulators of early progenitor and neuronal identities, as candidates for mediating this effect. Throughout the nervous system, levels of these miRNAs rise during the neurogenic period in progenitors, while levels in neurons correlate with their birth-date. Moreover, the sensitivity of tTF-encoding transcripts to miR-9 inversely correlates with their expression sequence, suggesting a model in which miR-9 controls the chronology of neuronal cell fate transitions by targeting specifiers of early progenitor and neuronal temporal identity in a level-dependent manner. Consistently, perturbations of miR-9 expression dynamics by gain and loss-of-function approaches perturb temporal patterning. Together, our results demonstrate a critical, evolutionary conserved role for miRNAs in temporal patterning and suggest that a temporal miR-9 expression gradient controls the timing of tTF expression in large parts of the developing vertebrate nervous system.

papers.title: Type I and III interferons differentially encode inflammatory gene activation through threshold control of ISGF3 dynamics
papers.abstract: Type I and type III interferons (IFNs) activate the shared Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway but generate distinct inflammatory transcriptional responses in addition to their shared antiviral transcriptional induction. While some mechanisms including cytokine-receptor affinity and receptor abundance have been proposed for regulating type I vs type III IFN specificity, they account for differences in signal amplitude but do not fully explain IFN-specific changes in JAK-STAT activity over time (i.e. the signaling temporal dynamics) which has been shown to be predictive of inflammatory gene activation. Here, we investigated mechanisms that could explain how type I and III IFNs produce distinct temporal dynamics of the IFN-activated transcription factor IFN-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3), leading to IFN-type specific activation of inflammatory genes in lung epithelial cells. We show that IFN-{beta}, a type I IFN, and IFN-{lambda}3, a type III IFN, induced comparable initial ISGF3 activation but subsequently generated distinct signaling trajectories, with IFN-{beta} undergoing potentiation and IFN-{lambda}3 limiting the duration of high ISGF3 activity, preventing robust inflammatory gene induction despite prolonged lower-level activity. Inflammatory gene induction was associated with the magnitude and duration of ISGF3 activity above an activation threshold during the intermediate phase of the signal response. The characteristic IFN-{lambda}3-induced ISGF3 signaling dynamics were maintained at saturating doses of IFN-{lambda}3 indicating the lack of signal activation above the threshold was independent of the dose. Additionally, differences in the abundance of the ISGF3 complex subunits STAT1, STAT2, and interferon regulatory factor 9 (IRF9), or in the induction of known negative regulators did not readily explain the response. Blocking protein synthesis caused rapid loss of IFN-{lambda}3-induced STAT phosphorylation and ISGF3 activity, supporting the presence of a pre-existing negative regulator limiting IFN-{lambda}3-mediated JAK-STAT pathway activation above the threshold required for activating inflammatory genes, while IFN-{beta} and IFN-{lambda}3 co-stimulation localized this regulation upstream of the shared ISGF3 complex. Increasing pathway competence through IFN-{beta} priming enhanced the IFN-{lambda}3-induced ISGF3 response above the inflammatory gene activation threshold leading to induction of inflammatory genes, albeit transiently. Together, these findings support a model in which the magnitude and duration of ISGF3 activity above an inflammatory gene activation threshold, rather than pathway activation alone, contribute to stimulus-specific transcriptional responses and suggest that a negative regulatory mechanism upstream of the ISGF3 complex constrains the temporal dynamics of IFN-{lambda}3 signaling.

papers.title: SIGMA: SIgnaling via Golgi Morphology Analysis for pathway-state classification
papers.abstract: Organelle morphology is increasingly recognized as a computationally accessible readout of molecular state, yet whether subcellular architecture can identify which signaling pathway is active, not merely whether a cell is perturbed, remains untested. Here we introduce SIGMA (SIgnaling via Golgi Morphology Analysis), a framework that reframes pathway identification as a morphological classification problem centered on the Golgi apparatus. SIGMA integrates imaging flow cytometry for population-scale Golgi profiling, teacher-student knowledge distillation to transfer fine morphological cues from limited high-resolution images to an efficient lower-resolution classifier, and mechanistic generalization testing with chemically distinct activators. Applied to MRC-5 fibroblasts across six conditions spanning four signaling cascades plus controls, SIGMA achieved 90.02% cell-level accuracy and correctly assigned five of seven structurally unrelated external compounds to their expected pathway class. These results establish Golgi morphology as a multiplexed, machine-readable fingerprint of signaling state.

papers.title: A miniature bioluminescent platform for imaging structured RNAs
papers.abstract: A broader understanding of RNA biology requires methods for visualizing transcript dynamics in native environments. Common imaging approaches rely on fluorescent probes that require excitation light and often depend on large aptamer arrays, limiting sensitivity and compatibility with many non-coding RNAs, particularly highly structured folds. To address these challenges, we developed a miniaturized bioluminescent platform for RNA imaging. This system employs a compact RNA tag that assembles luciferase fragments upon binding of monomeric RNA-binding proteins (RNA lanterns). Systematic optimization of the RNA component yielded a structured 24-nucleotide tag, representing greater than 3-fold reduction in size relative to the original C-11-B RNA tag, placing it among the smallest RNA imaging tags reported to date. The optimized tag enabled RNA-dependent bioluminescence detection in live cells, notably as a small, single insert within highly structured non-coding RNAs, including the MALAT1 ENE domain and a small HDV-like ribozyme. Collectively, this work establishes a miniaturized bioluminescent platform for imaging a broad range of RNA targets in living systems.
